item.title: Congenital Nevus Removal: Large Birthmark Excision
item.dc:creator: Vijayan
item.content:encoded:
Congenital Nevus Removal: Expert Surgical Options

This guide covers the motivations for removing large birthmarks, from managing melanoma risk to addressing aesthetic concerns. We will explore surgical techniques like full-thickness and staged excision, offering specific details on recovery timelines and aftercare. By focusing on managing expectations around scarring and the final aesthetic outcome, we provide a clear overview of the patient journey from assessment to treatment, a perspective often overlooked in other resources.

As a Consultant Plastic Surgeon, Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), emphasises a collaborative and patient-centred approach. His extensive experience in both the NHS and private practice across London and Hertfordshire ensures you receive compassionate, expert care tailored to your unique needs. To explore your treatment options and discuss a bespoke solution, we invite you to Book Now a one-on-one consultation.

Table of Contents

  • What Are Congenital Melanocytic Nevi?
  • Should Congenital Nevi Be Removed?
  • Assessing Cancer Risk in Large Birthmarks
  • Non-Surgical Options for Pigmented Birthmarks
  • Congenital Nevus Removal: Surgical Techniques
  • What Is Recovery Like After Birthmark Excision?
  • What Results Can I Expect From Staged Nevus Removal?
  • Congenital Nevus Removal in London & Hertfordshire

What Are Congenital Melanocytic Nevi?

The decision to pursue congenital nevus removal often begins with understanding exactly what these birthmarks are. A congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a specific type of pigmented birthmark, or mole, that is present at birth or appears within the first few weeks of life. These nevi are formed by a benign overgrowth of melanocytes, the cells that produce pigment (melanin) in the skin. Their appearance can vary significantly in colour, from light brown to almost black, and they may have a flat, raised, or even lumpy texture. Some may also have excess hair growth.

Plastic surgeons classify CMN primarily by their projected adult size, as this has implications for both monitoring and potential treatment. The classifications are:

  • Small Congenital Nevi: Less than 1.5 cm in diameter.
  • Medium Congenital Nevi: Between 1.5 cm and 19.9 cm in diameter.
  • Large or Giant Congenital Nevi (GCMN): 20 cm or greater in diameter. Giant nevi can sometimes cover extensive areas of the body, such as the entire torso (known as a "bathing trunk" nevus) or a limb.

Whilst small and medium nevi are relatively common, large and giant nevi are much rarer. The management approach, including the consideration for birthmark removal surgery, is highly individualised and depends on the nevus's size, location, and specific characteristics, as well as the patient's age and the medical and psychosocial factors involved. A detailed assessment with a specialist plastic surgeon is the essential first step in creating a safe and appropriate management plan.

Should Congenital Nevi Be Removed?

The decision to remove a congenital nevus is based on a careful balance of medical and personal factors. Medically, removal is considered to reduce the lifelong risk of melanoma, a type of skin cancer, which is higher in larger nevi. Psychosocially, removal can alleviate distress related to the birthmark's appearance.

Key reasons for considering congenital nevus removal include:

  • Melanoma Risk Reduction: This is the primary medical reason. Removing the nevus cells eliminates the tissue from which a melanoma could potentially develop. The risk is most significant with large and giant congenital nevi.
  • Easier Skin Monitoring: Large, dark, or irregular nevi can make it difficult to spot new or changing lesions. Removing the nevus simplifies future skin surveillance for both the patient and their doctors.
  • Symptomatic Relief: Some nevi can be prone to itching, dryness, or irritation, or may be located in areas of high friction (like a waistband or bra strap). Excision can resolve these physical symptoms.
  • Improved Aesthetic Appearance: For many patients and parents, the cosmetic appearance of a prominent birthmark is a significant concern. Surgery aims to replace the nevus with a more subtle scar, improving the contour and colour of the skin.
  • Psychosocial Well-being: A visible birthmark can affect self-esteem and confidence, particularly during childhood and adolescence. Removal may be considered to mitigate potential social anxiety or teasing.
  • Functional Improvement: In rare cases, a nevus on an eyelid, lip, or joint may interfere with function. Surgical removal can restore normal function to the affected area.

Assessing Cancer Risk in Large Birthmarks

One of the most pressing concerns for patients and parents is the risk of malignant transformation—the nevus developing into a melanoma. It is vital to approach this topic with clarity and perspective. The lifetime risk of developing melanoma within a congenital nevus is directly related to its size. For small and medium-sized nevi, the lifetime risk is considered to be very low, estimated at less than 1%.

The risk increases significantly with large and giant congenital melanocytic nevi (GCMN). Whilst exact figures are debated in medical literature, the estimated lifetime risk for patients with GCMN is often cited as being between 2% and 5%. Importantly, in these larger nevi, melanoma can sometimes develop deeper within the tissue, not just on the surface, making early detection more challenging. This is a key reason why prophylactic congenital mole removal is more frequently discussed for larger birthmarks.

Regardless of any decision about surgical removal, regular monitoring is paramount. This involves:

  • Self-Examination: Patients or parents should regularly check the nevus for any changes in size, shape, colour, or texture. Any new lumps, bumps, ulceration, or bleeding should be reported to a doctor immediately.
  • Professional Review: Regular follow-up with a dermatologist or plastic surgeon is crucial. They can perform a detailed examination, sometimes using a dermatoscope for a magnified view of the pigment patterns.
  • Clinical Photography: A photographic record of the nevus allows for objective comparison over time, helping to identify subtle changes that might otherwise be missed.

During your consultation, we will have a frank and open discussion about the specific risk profile of your or your child's nevus, ensuring you have a clear understanding upon which to base your decisions.

Non-Surgical Options for Pigmented Birthmarks

When exploring treatment for a congenital nevus, patients often ask about non-surgical alternatives. Whilst techniques such as laser therapy, dermabrasion, and chemical peels exist for pigmented lesions, their role in managing congenital melanocytic nevi is limited and comes with significant caveats. It is crucial to understand that these methods are often cosmetic in nature and do not address the underlying medical concerns associated with CMN.

These treatments work by targeting the pigment in the upper layers of the skin. However, congenital nevi are not just a surface-level discolouration; the nevus cells extend deep into the dermis (the lower layer of skin) and sometimes even into the subcutaneous fat beneath. Non-surgical methods cannot reliably remove these deeper cells.

Limitations of Non-Surgical Approaches:

  • Incomplete Removal: As these methods only treat the surface, the deep nevus cells remain. This means the pigment can, and often does, return over time.
  • No Reduction in Cancer Risk: Because the nevus cells are not fully removed, the underlying risk of malignant transformation is not eliminated. Furthermore, the resulting scar tissue and pigment changes can make future melanoma surveillance more difficult.
  • Risk of Scarring: Aggressive laser treatment or dermabrasion can cause significant scarring, which may be less aesthetically pleasing than a planned surgical scar.

For these reasons, pigmented birthmark surgery through full-thickness excision remains the gold standard for the definitive removal of a congenital nevus. Non-surgical options are generally not recommended as a primary treatment by plastic surgeons for true congenital melanocytic nevi, as they fail to achieve the main goals of treatment: complete removal of the nevus cells and reduction of long-term risk.

Congenital Nevus Removal: Surgical Techniques

Surgical excision is the most effective method for the complete removal of a congenital nevus. As a consultant plastic surgeon, my approach is to select the technique that will achieve the best possible outcome whilst prioritising safety and minimising scarring. The chosen strategy depends heavily on the nevus's size, location, and the laxity of the surrounding skin.

Full-Thickness Excision with Direct Closure

For small and some medium-sized nevi, a single operation is often sufficient. The procedure involves surgically excising the entire thickness of the nevus down to the underlying fat layer, ensuring all nevus cells are removed. The surrounding skin is then carefully mobilised and closed in layers with fine sutures to create a neat, linear scar. This is similar to surgical excision techniques for pigmented lesions of other types. The excised tissue is always sent for histopathological analysis to confirm the diagnosis and ensure no abnormal cells are present.

Staged Excision

When a nevus is too large to be removed and closed in one go, a staged excision is the preferred approach. This involves a series of planned operations, typically spaced 3 to 6 months apart. In each stage, a portion of the nevus (usually the central part first) is removed, and the wound is closed. This allows the surrounding healthy skin to stretch and relax between procedures. Over several stages, the entire nevus is progressively removed and replaced by a series of joined surgical scars.

Staged Excision with Tissue Expanders

For very large or giant nevi, especially on the scalp, forehead, or trunk, there may not be enough adjacent skin to allow for staged excision alone. In these complex cases, tissue expansion is an invaluable technique. This process involves a preliminary operation to place a temporary, balloon-like device (an expander) under the healthy skin next to the nevus. Over several weeks, the expander is gradually inflated with saline solution during outpatient visits, causing the overlying skin to stretch and grow, much like the skin of the abdomen expands during pregnancy. Once enough new skin has been created, a second major operation is performed to remove the expander, excise the nevus, and use the newly generated skin flap to cover the defect. This advanced reconstructive technique, often performed within the NHS for complex cases, allows for the replacement of the nevus with skin of a similar colour and texture. As an experienced plastic surgeon, Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), is skilled in assessing which of these techniques is most appropriate for each individual case.

What Is Recovery Like After Birthmark Excision?

Understanding the recovery process is a vital part of preparing for birthmark excision. The specifics will vary depending on the surgical technique used, the size and location of the nevus, and the age of the patient, but a general timeline can be provided. My team and I will ensure you have detailed, personalised instructions for your aftercare.

Immediately after the procedure, the wound will be closed with sutures and covered with a protective dressing. For smaller excisions, this may be a simple sterile dressing, whilst larger excisions or those involving tissue expansion may require more substantial bandages. Some discomfort is expected, but this is typically well-managed with simple painkillers like paracetamol or ibuprofen. You will receive clear guidance on wound care, which usually involves keeping the area clean and dry for the first few days.

Typical Recovery Milestones:

  • First 48-72 Hours: This is a period of rest. You should limit strenuous activity to minimise swelling and strain on the sutures. Keeping the surgical site elevated, if possible, can also help.
  • 1-2 Weeks: The initial healing phase. Dissolvable sutures will disappear on their own, whilst non-dissolvable stitches are typically removed in the clinic between 7 and 14 days after surgery. Most children and adults can return to school or desk-based work within a week, though contact sports and swimming must be avoided.
  • 2-6 Weeks: The scar will be pink and slightly raised, which is a normal part of healing. You can gradually resume most normal activities, but heavy lifting and activities that significantly stretch the scar should still be avoided. We will advise you on when it is safe to begin gentle scar massage with a simple moisturiser.
  • 6 Months to 1 Year+: This is the scar maturation phase. The scar will gradually fade, soften, and flatten. Protecting the new scar from direct sun exposure with high-SPF sunscreen is absolutely essential for at least a year to prevent it from becoming permanently darkened.

Follow-up appointments are a crucial part of the process, allowing us to monitor your healing and provide guidance on scar management to ensure the best possible long-term result.

What Results Can I Expect From Staged Nevus Removal?

Managing expectations is one of the most important aspects of my consultation process for congenital nevus removal. It is essential to understand that the goal of surgery is not to create "perfect" or invisible skin. The goal is to replace the nevus with a surgical scar that is, in most cases, more aesthetically acceptable and socially inconspicuous than the original birthmark, whilst also removing the associated medical risks.

Surgery can and should achieve the following:

  • Complete removal of the congenital nevus cells.
  • A significant improvement in the skin's contour and uniformity.
  • Replacement of the dark pigmentation with a scar that will mature and fade over time.

What surgery cannot achieve is the complete erasure of any sign that the nevus was there. There will always be a permanent scar. The quality of this final scar depends on many factors, including the location of the nevus (scars on joints or high-tension areas like the back and shoulders tend to be wider), your individual genetic healing response, and, crucially, how well you follow the aftercare instructions. For a staged nevus removal, the final result will be a series of joined scars that mark the boundaries of each excision stage.

As a specialist plastic surgeon, Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), uses meticulous surgical techniques to place scars in natural skin creases where possible and to minimise tension on the closure. During the healing phase, we provide guidance on scar care, which may include silicone gel or sheets and massage. Over the course of 12-18 months, the scar will mature, transitioning from pink and raised to a paler, flatter line. In cases where a scar is suboptimal, further treatments like scar revision can be considered at a later date. The ultimate aim is a result that you or your child can feel confident and comfortable with.

Congenital Nevus Removal in London & Hertfordshire

Deciding on treatment for a congenital nevus is a significant step for any individual or family. My practice is founded on providing a supportive, informative, and collaborative environment where you can explore your options without pressure. During a comprehensive consultation, I will perform a thorough assessment, discuss the benefits and risks of each approach, and help you understand the realistic outcomes you can expect from congenital nevus removal.

My focus is always on creating a personalised treatment plan that aligns with your specific goals, whether they are primarily medical, cosmetic, or both. With a deep understanding of advanced reconstructive techniques, including staged excisions and tissue expansion, I am committed to achieving the safest and most effective result for every patient.

To discuss your options with Mr. Vijayan, book a personal consultation at his practice serving patients across London, Hertfordshire, and Stevenage.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best age for congenital nevus removal?

The optimal timing for congenital nevus removal depends on the nevus size, location, and associated melanoma risk. For most nevi, surgery is often considered between six months of age and puberty to balance anaesthetic safety with the psychological benefits of early treatment.

Operating on infants under six months carries slightly higher anaesthetic risks. Conversely, waiting until adolescence can present psychosocial challenges for the child. A consultation allows for a personalised assessment to determine the most appropriate surgical plan and timing for your child's specific situation.

When is staged excision recommended over a single surgery?

Staged excision is the standard approach for large or giant congenital nevi where the birthmark is too extensive to be removed and closed in a single operation. This technique allows the surrounding healthy skin to stretch, providing sufficient tissue for a tension-free closure.

Attempting to remove a very large nevus at once could lead to significant skin tension, distortion of nearby features (like an eye or the mouth), and poor scarring. By removing the nevus in planned stages, we can achieve a more controlled and aesthetically favourable outcome.

Who should manage a large congenital nevus: a plastic surgeon or a dermatologist?

While dermatologists are experts in diagnosing and monitoring skin lesions, a consultant plastic surgeon is best equipped to perform the surgical removal of large congenital nevi. This is due to the complex reconstructive techniques often required for an optimal functional and aesthetic result.

The excision of a large nevus is a reconstructive challenge. It requires advanced skills in tissue handling, skin grafting, flap surgery, or the use of tissue expanders to close the resulting defect. A plastic surgeon’s training focuses specifically on these techniques to restore form and minimise scarring.

What are tissue expanders and how are they used in nevus removal?

A tissue expander is a medical-grade silicone balloon that is placed under healthy skin adjacent to the large nevus. Over several weeks, it is gradually inflated with saline, encouraging the overlying skin to stretch and create new tissue for reconstruction.

Once enough new skin has been generated, a second operation is performed to remove the expander and the nevus. The newly created skin flap is then used to cover the defect, which often produces a superior aesthetic result compared to a skin graft.

How much does congenital nevus removal cost?

The cost of congenital nevus removal varies significantly based on the size and complexity of the nevus, the surgical technique required, and whether it is a single or multi-stage procedure. A detailed quotation is always provided following a full consultation and clinical assessment.

The final fee typically includes the surgeon's fee, anaesthetist's fee, and hospital facility charges. Mr. Vijayan’s team will provide a transparent breakdown of all anticipated costs as part of your personalised treatment plan.

item.title: Breast Lift Complications: Risks and How to Minimize Them
item.dc:creator: Vijayan
item.content:encoded:
Breast Lift Complications: Understanding Mastopexy Risks

Understanding breast lift complications is a vital part of your surgical journey. This guide details specific mastopexy risks and provides important context on their frequency and management. We will explore your role in minimising side effects before and after surgery, discuss long-term results and scar maturation, and clarify how your choice of surgeon contributes to a safe outcome. You will gain a clear perspective on what to expect and how to prepare for a smooth recovery.

Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), is a Consultant Plastic Surgeon who brings extensive experience from his NHS consultant post in Stevenage. To discuss your options with Mr. Roshan Vijayan, book a personal consultation at his practice serving patients across London, Hertfordshire, and Stevenage.

Table of Contents

  • What Are the Main Risks of Mastopexy Surgery?
  • How Common Are Breast Lift Complications?
  • Am I a Good Candidate for a Safe Breast Lift?
  • How to Minimise Your Breast Lift Side Effects
  • Long-Term Results and Scar Maturation After a Lift
  • The Role of an NHS-Experienced Surgeon in Hertfordshire
  • Discuss Your Breast Lift in London with Mr Roshan Vijayan

What Are the Main Risks of Mastopexy Surgery?

Understanding the potential breast lift complications is a fundamental step in making an informed decision about your procedure. While mastopexy is a commonly performed and generally safe surgery, like any surgical intervention, it carries inherent risks. A thorough consultation will explore these possibilities in the context of your personal health profile. For an overview of the procedure itself, you can find the full procedural details on our website. The main mastopexy risks can be categorised into specific surgical complications and general risks associated with any operation.

Scarring

Scars are an unavoidable outcome of a breast lift. The extent and location of the scars depend on the technique used to achieve your desired breast shape. While they are placed as discreetly as possible, their final appearance varies between individuals. Most scars fade significantly over 12 to 18 months, but some patients may experience prominent, raised (hypertrophic or keloid) scarring. Following post-operative scar care advice is vital for achieving the best possible outcome.

Infection

Wound infection is an uncommon risk, occurring in a small percentage of cases. It is typically managed effectively with a course of antibiotics. Signs include increased redness, swelling, pain, or discharge from the incision sites. Adhering strictly to your surgeon's pre- and post-operative hygiene instructions is the most effective way to minimise this risk.

Bleeding and Haematoma

Some post-operative bleeding or bruising is normal. A haematoma, a collection of blood under the skin, is a less frequent complication that may cause swelling and discomfort. Small haematomas often resolve on their own, but a larger one might require a minor procedure to be drained to alleviate pressure and aid healing.

Asymmetry

Most women have some degree of pre-existing breast asymmetry. While the goal of surgery is to improve symmetry, it is not always possible to achieve a completely identical appearance. Minor differences in breast shape, size, or nipple position can persist or occur as a result of the healing process. In rare cases, a significant asymmetry might warrant a revision procedure.

Sensation Changes

Temporary numbness or altered sensation in the nipples and breast skin is common after a breast lift. For most patients, normal sensation gradually returns over several months as the nerves heal. However, in a small number of cases, these changes can be permanent. This risk will be discussed in detail during your consultation.

General Surgical and Anaesthetic Risks

As with any surgery performed under general anaesthesia, there are broader risks such as adverse reactions to anaesthetic agents, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and pulmonary embolism. These risks are low in healthy individuals and are carefully managed by the anaesthetist and surgical team throughout the procedure and recovery period.

How Common Are Breast Lift Complications?

Breast lift complications are not common when the procedure is performed by a qualified plastic surgeon on a suitable candidate. While minor issues like temporary bruising and swelling are expected side effects, significant mastopexy complications are infrequent. The overall risk is managed through careful patient selection and meticulous surgical technique.

The most common issues you should be aware of include:

  • Unsatisfactory Scarring: Scars are expected, but problematic scarring (e.g., hypertrophic or keloid) is a possibility, influenced by genetics and aftercare.
  • Infection: Occurs in a very small percentage of cases and is usually treated simply with antibiotics.
  • Haematoma: A collection of blood under the skin that may require drainage. This is also an uncommon event.
  • Asymmetry: Minor differences between the breasts are common both before and after surgery. Significant asymmetry requiring revision is rare.
  • Nipple Sensation Changes: Temporary numbness is common, but permanent loss of sensation is an infrequent risk.
  • Delayed Wound Healing: More prevalent in smokers or patients with certain medical conditions.

Am I a Good Candidate for a Safe Breast Lift?

A key factor in ensuring breast lift safety is patient suitability. A responsible surgeon will conduct a thorough assessment to determine if a mastopexy is the appropriate and safe choice for you. The ideal candidate is an individual who is in good general health, both physically and mentally, and who has realistic expectations about the surgical outcome. Certain factors can increase surgical risks, and it is crucial to be open about your medical history during your consultation.

Key characteristics of a good candidate include:

  • Being in good physical health: You should be free from any serious medical conditions that could impair healing or increase the risks of surgery.
  • Being a non-smoker: Smoking significantly compromises blood flow to the skin, which can lead to delayed healing, tissue loss, and more prominent scarring. You will be required to stop smoking for a significant period before and after your operation.
  • Having a stable weight: Significant weight fluctuations after a breast lift can alter the shape and position of the breasts, compromising the surgical results. It is best to be at or near your target weight before undergoing the procedure.
  • Having realistic expectations: It is important to understand what a breast lift can and cannot do. It repositions and reshapes the breast tissue but does not significantly increase breast size.
  • Considering future pregnancies: While it is possible to breastfeed after a lift, the results of the surgery can be affected by subsequent pregnancies. For this reason, some women choose to wait until they have finished having children. A breast lift can also be performed as part of a mummy makeover.

A detailed discussion with your surgeon will confirm your suitability and allow for a personalised treatment plan that prioritises your safety and desired results.

How to Minimise Your Breast Lift Side Effects

While your surgeon is responsible for performing the procedure safely, you play an active and vital role in minimising your breast lift side effects and overall risks. Your cooperation and adherence to medical advice before and after the operation are crucial for a smooth recovery and a satisfactory outcome. This partnership between patient and surgeon is the foundation of a safe and successful surgical journey.

Before Your Surgery

Preparation begins weeks before the procedure. To prepare your body for surgery and healing, you will be advised to stop smoking and vaping at least six weeks prior. You should also avoid certain medications and supplements, such as aspirin, anti-inflammatory drugs, and some herbal remedies that can increase bleeding. Providing a complete and honest medical history allows your surgical team to anticipate and manage any potential risks effectively. It is your responsibility to follow these pre-operative instructions precisely.

After Your Surgery

The post-operative period is when your actions have the most direct impact on your healing. This includes taking prescribed medications, such as antibiotics or pain relief, exactly as directed. You must care for your incisions according to the specific instructions provided to prevent infection and support healing. Wearing your surgical support bra consistently is essential for reducing swelling and supporting the new breast shape. Attending all scheduled follow-up appointments is also non-negotiable; these allow your surgeon to monitor your progress, identify any potential issues early, and guide you on when it is safe to resume normal activities, including exercise.

Long-Term Results and Scar Maturation After a Lift

The results of a breast lift are designed to be long-lasting, providing a more youthful and elevated breast contour. However, it is important to understand that the procedure does not stop the natural ageing process. Over many years, factors such as gravity, skin elasticity changes, and hormonal shifts will continue to affect the breast's appearance. The longevity of your results can be maximised by maintaining a stable weight and a healthy lifestyle. Significant weight gain or loss after surgery can stretch the skin and alter the shape of the breasts.

Future pregnancies and breastfeeding can also have a substantial impact on the results, potentially leading to further sagging. For this reason, many patients choose to undergo a mastopexy after they have completed their family.

Scars are a permanent part of the procedure, but their appearance will change significantly over time. Initially, they may appear red and slightly raised. Over the course of 12 to 18 months, they typically soften, flatten, and fade to a much lighter colour. The process of Scar maturation is different for everyone and is influenced by genetics and how well you follow post-operative scar care protocols. Protecting scars from sun exposure for at least the first year is crucial to prevent them from darkening permanently.

The Role of an NHS-Experienced Surgeon in Hertfordshire

Choosing the right surgeon is the single most important decision you can make to ensure your safety and the quality of your result. Your surgeon should not only be skilled in the specific procedure but also hold the requisite qualifications and experience. Look for a surgeon on the GMC Specialist Register for Plastic Surgery and one who is a member of professional bodies like BAAPS or BAPRAS.

Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), is a Consultant Plastic Surgeon with extensive experience in both the NHS and private practice. His role as an NHS Consultant based in Stevenage means he is accustomed to the highest standards of clinical governance, patient safety protocols, and multidisciplinary care. This background provides a robust foundation for his private work with patients from Hertfordshire, London, and beyond.

Working within the NHS requires managing a diverse range of complex cases, which hones a surgeon's diagnostic and technical skills. This experience is directly transferable to cosmetic surgery, ensuring a comprehensive and considered approach to every patient's care plan. You can learn more about Mr Roshan Vijayan's background and his commitment to patient-centred care, which is built on a career dedicated to the principles of safety and excellence upheld by the National Health Service.

Discuss Your Breast Lift in London with Mr Roshan Vijayan

Navigating the information about a breast lift can feel overwhelming. The most effective way to understand the benefits and risks as they apply to you is through a direct, one-to-one consultation with a specialist. This appointment provides the opportunity to ask detailed questions, view before and after photos of previous patients, and receive a professional assessment of your suitability for the procedure. Mr. Roshan Vijayan prioritises a clear and honest dialogue, ensuring you have all the information you need to move forward with confidence.

To discuss your options with Mr. Roshan Vijayan, book a personal consultation at his practice serving patients across London, Hertfordshire, and Stevenage.

FAQs About the Dangers and Safety of Breast Lifts

Is breast lift surgery safe?

A mastopexy is a common surgical procedure with a well-established safety profile when performed by a qualified consultant plastic surgeon. While all surgery carries inherent risks, such as those related to anaesthesia and infection, significant breast lift complications are infrequent for healthy, well-selected patients.

Your surgeon will conduct a thorough medical assessment to confirm your suitability for the procedure and discuss the specific risks with you.

Will my breast lift results last forever?

A breast lift provides long-lasting results by surgically repositioning breast tissue. However, the procedure does not stop the natural ageing process. Factors such as significant weight fluctuations, future pregnancies, and gravity will continue to affect the breasts' shape and position over time.

Maintaining a stable weight can help to preserve your results for as long as possible.

Can I have a breast lift if I plan to have more children?

While surgically possible, it is generally advisable to wait until you have completed your family before undergoing a breast lift. Future pregnancies and breastfeeding can significantly alter the size and shape of the breasts, which may compromise the surgical outcome and create a need for revision surgery.

When can I return to exercise after a mastopexy?

Patients are typically advised to avoid strenuous exercise and heavy lifting for four to six weeks following a mastopexy. Gentle walking is encouraged soon after surgery to promote circulation, but high-impact activities must be reintroduced gradually, based on your surgeon's specific guidance for your recovery.

What happens during a breast lift consultation?

Your initial consultation is a detailed discussion about your aesthetic goals and medical history. Mr. Vijayan will perform a physical examination, explain the surgical technique, discuss potential outcomes and risks, and show you representative before-and-after photos to help manage your expectations.

This is your opportunity to ask any questions you may have.

How much does a breast lift cost?

The cost of a breast lift depends on the surgical technique required, hospital fees, and anaesthetist's charges. A precise, all-inclusive quotation will be provided following your personal consultation, once your individual surgical plan has been established. This bespoke quotation ensures there are no hidden costs.

item.title: Seborrheic Keratosis Removal: Cosmetic Lesion Treatment
item.dc:creator: Vijayan
item.content:encoded:
Seborrheic Keratosis Removal: A Consultant's Guide

Seborrheic keratosis removal is a common procedure for benign skin lesions. This guide explains what these growths are, how they are diagnosed to distinguish them from other conditions, and the various treatment options available. It also provides a detailed comparison of removal methods and clarifies the specific role a plastic surgeon plays in achieving a desirable cosmetic result, ensuring you have realistic expectations for your outcome.

Mr. Roshan Vijayan is a Consultant Plastic Surgeon, FRCS (Plast), who holds a substantive NHS consultant post in Stevenage. To discuss your options with Mr. Roshan Vijayan, book a personal consultation at his practice serving patients across London, Hertfordshire, and Stevenage.

Table of Contents

  • What Are These Common, Harmless Skin Growths?
  • Distinguishing Seborrheic Keratosis From Skin Cancer
  • Why Consider Seborrheic Keratosis Removal?
  • Your Treatment Options for Seborrheic Keratosis Removal
  • The SK Removal Procedure: What to Expect on the Day
  • What Does Recovery and Aftercare Involve?
  • Realistic Outcomes After Your Lesion Removal in Hertfordshire
  • Arranging Your Consultation for Benign Lesion Removal

What Are These Common, Harmless Skin Growths?

Seborrheic keratoses (singular: keratosis) are benign, non-cancerous skin growths that are very common, particularly in individuals over the age of 40. Often referred to as senile warts or basal cell papillomas, these lesions are harmless and do not have the potential to become malignant.

They typically have a characteristic 'stuck-on' appearance, looking as if a small piece of wax has been applied to the skin. Their appearance can vary significantly. They may be light tan, brown, or almost black in colour. The texture is often waxy, scaly, and slightly elevated from the skin's surface. They can range in size from a few millimetres to several centimetres and may appear as a single lesion or in clusters. Common areas for seborrheic keratoses to develop include the chest, back, stomach, scalp, face, and neck. While their exact cause is not fully understood, they tend to run in families and become more numerous with age. Sun exposure may also play a role in their development. Crucially, they are not contagious and are not caused by a virus.

Distinguishing Seborrheic Keratosis From Skin Cancer

While seborrheic keratoses are entirely benign, their appearance can sometimes cause concern because they may share visual characteristics with certain types of skin cancer, such as malignant melanoma. Differentiating between a harmless growth and a potentially dangerous one requires a trained clinical eye, and self-diagnosis should be avoided. A formal assessment is the only way to achieve diagnostic certainty.

Typically, seborrheic keratoses have a well-defined border and a waxy, 'pasted-on' look that distinguishes them from other lesions. However, certain features should prompt a professional evaluation to rule out malignancy. These include rapid changes in size, shape, or colour; the development of an irregular border; a lesion that becomes itchy, painful, or starts to bleed or crust without being irritated. On occasion, a skin cancer can arise next to or within an existing seborrheic keratosis, which can complicate visual assessment.

If there is any diagnostic uncertainty during your consultation, the lesion may be sent for histopathological analysis after removal. This microscopic examination provides a definitive diagnosis. It is always the safest approach when a lesion presents with atypical features. This is a similar protocol to that used for suspicious mole removal, where caution and thorough analysis are paramount.

Why Consider Seborrheic Keratosis Removal?

The decision for seborrheic keratosis removal is almost always driven by cosmetic preference or physical discomfort, rather than medical necessity. Since these growths are benign, they do not pose a health risk if left untreated. However, there are several compelling reasons why individuals choose to have them removed.

From a cosmetic standpoint, seborrheic keratoses can be a source of self-consciousness, especially when they appear in prominent locations such as the face, neck, or hands. They can affect one's confidence in social or professional settings. Their dark colour and raised texture can make them difficult to conceal with makeup, leading many to seek a permanent solution.

Physical irritation is another common reason for removal. Depending on their location, these lesions can catch on clothing or jewellery, leading to friction, inflammation, and occasional bleeding. Those located in skin folds, such as under the breasts or in the groin, can become sweaty and irritated. Shaving can also be problematic if the lesions are on the face, scalp or legs, as they may be repeatedly nicked by a razor. In these instances, removing the lesion can significantly improve daily comfort. While treatment is not usually available on the NHS for purely cosmetic reasons, private removal offers a direct and effective solution.

Your Treatment Options for Seborrheic Keratosis Removal

Several effective methods are available for seborrheic keratosis removal, and the best option depends on the lesion's size, location, thickness, and your cosmetic goals. As a Consultant Plastic Surgeon, Mr. Roshan Vijayan prioritises techniques that minimise scarring and achieve a pleasing aesthetic result. The choice of technique is discussed in detail during your consultation.

Comparing Removal Methods

  • Curettage and Cautery: This is a frequently used method for seborrheic keratoses. After numbing the area with local anaesthetic, the lesion is gently scraped off the skin's surface using a spoon-shaped instrument called a curette. A light electrical current (cautery) is then used to stop any minor bleeding and smooth the skin base. This technique is highly effective and typically results in minimal scarring.
  • Shave Excision: Similar to curettage, this involves using a fine surgical blade to shave the lesion off at the level of the surrounding skin. It is also performed under local anaesthetic and is an excellent option for raised lesions. The resulting wound is shallow and usually heals very well with a low risk of noticeable scarring.
  • Cryotherapy: This involves applying liquid nitrogen to the lesion to freeze and destroy the cells. The treated area will blister and then scab over before falling off within a few weeks. While effective for very flat, small lesions, cryotherapy offers less precision than surgical methods and carries a higher risk of pigmentary changes (lightening or darkening of the skin), particularly in individuals with darker skin tones.

Plastic Surgeon vs. Dermatologist

While both dermatologists and plastic surgeons are highly skilled in skin lesion treatments, a plastic surgeon brings a specific focus on optimising the cosmetic outcome. Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), applies principles of plastic surgery to every procedure, using meticulous techniques to minimise scarring and align any incisions with natural skin creases. This approach is particularly valuable for lesions on the face, neck, and other highly visible areas where the final aesthetic result is of utmost importance. The goal is not just to remove the lesion, but to restore the skin to its most natural state. For more information about other skin lesion treatments offered, please see our main skin procedures page.

The SK Removal Procedure: What to Expect on the Day

Your seborrheic keratosis removal will be performed as a straightforward outpatient procedure, meaning you can return home the same day. The entire process is designed to be as comfortable and efficient as possible. Upon arrival at the clinic, you will be welcomed and prepared for your treatment.

The first step in the SK removal procedure involves a final confirmation of the lesion to be removed and answering any last-minute questions you may have. The skin around the seborrheic keratosis will be thoroughly cleansed with an antiseptic solution to minimise the risk of infection. Mr. Vijayan will then administer a small injection of local anaesthetic directly into the treatment area. You may feel a brief stinging sensation as the anaesthetic is injected, but the area will become completely numb within moments, ensuring the rest of the procedure is painless.

Once the area is numb, the chosen removal method—typically curettage and cautery or shave excision—will be performed. You will not feel any pain during this part, though you might be aware of gentle pressure or movement. The process is usually very quick, often taking only a few minutes per lesion. After the lesion is removed, a light dressing or a simple ointment will be applied to the area to protect it. You will then be provided with detailed aftercare instructions before being discharged.

What Does Recovery and Aftercare Involve?

The recovery period following the removal of a seborrheic keratosis is generally short and uncomplicated. Proper aftercare is essential for ensuring swift healing and achieving the best possible cosmetic result. You will receive specific, personalised instructions, but the general principles of care are consistent.

Immediately after the procedure, the treated area will look like a small graze or superficial scrape. A simple dressing may be applied, which you might be asked to keep clean and dry for the first 24-48 hours. After this initial period, you can usually wash the area gently with mild soap and water. Pat the area dry carefully; do not rub it. Applying a thin layer of an antiseptic or petroleum-based ointment, as recommended, can help keep the wound moist, which promotes better healing and can reduce the final visibility of any scar.

A scab will form over the site within a few days. It is vital that you allow this scab to fall off on its own. Picking at it can introduce bacteria, increase the risk of infection, and lead to more prominent scarring. The healing process typically takes one to three weeks, depending on the size and location of the removed lesion. During this time, and for several months afterwards, protecting the healing skin from sun exposure is critical. Applying a high-SPF sunscreen (SPF 50+) daily will help prevent hyperpigmentation (darkening) of the new skin, ensuring it blends more naturally with the surrounding tissue.

Realistic Outcomes After Your Lesion Removal in Hertfordshire

Seeking seborrheic keratosis or age spots removal is primarily a cosmetic undertaking, and it is important to have clear expectations about the results. The goal of the treatment is to remove the raised, pigmented lesion and leave behind a smoother, more uniform skin surface. While modern techniques are highly effective and aim for minimal scarring, no procedure that breaks the skin is entirely without a trace.

Immediately after healing, the new skin at the treatment site may appear pink or red. This is a normal part of the healing process and this colour will gradually fade over several weeks to months. The final appearance of the skin can take up to a year to fully mature. In most cases, the result is a small, flat mark that is significantly less noticeable than the original lesion. For many patients, it blends in so well with the surrounding skin that it is difficult to spot.

However, some potential for pigmentary changes exists. The treated area may heal slightly lighter (hypopigmentation) or darker (hyperpigmentation) than the surrounding skin. This is an uncommon outcome but is seen more frequently in individuals with darker skin types and can be exacerbated by sun exposure during the healing phase. Mr. Roshan Vijayan, an experienced NHS Consultant Plastic Surgeon, will discuss these possibilities with you during your consultation, ensuring you have a comprehensive understanding of what your treatment can realistically achieve.

Arranging Your Consultation for Benign Lesion Removal

The first step towards addressing unwanted skin lesions is a thorough consultation. This appointment provides an opportunity for a definitive diagnosis and a detailed discussion about your concerns and aesthetic goals. During this session, the lesion will be carefully examined to confirm that it is a seborrheic keratosis and to rule out any other conditions.

You will be able to discuss the different methods for benign lesion removal and receive a professional recommendation for the technique best suited to your specific case. This is your time to ask questions about the procedure, recovery, potential risks, and expected outcomes. A personalised treatment plan will be created for you, along with a clear outline of the associated costs. The consultation ensures you have all the information needed to make a confident and informed decision about your care with Mr. Roshan Vijayan.

To discuss your options with Mr. Roshan Vijayan, book a personal consultation at his practice serving patients across London, Hertfordshire, and Stevenage.

Frequently Asked Questions About Seborrheic Keratosis

Do seborrheic keratoses grow back after removal?

A completely removed seborrheic keratosis will not typically recur in the exact same location. However, individuals prone to these growths may develop new, separate lesions on other areas of the skin over time. This is due to a predisposition, not a failure of the initial treatment.

Is the removal procedure painful?

Procedures are performed using a local anaesthetic to numb the treatment area completely. While you may feel a minor sting from the initial injection, the removal process itself should be comfortable and free of pain. Any mild discomfort following the procedure can usually be managed with standard painkillers.

Will I have a scar after the removal?

Any procedure that penetrates the skin carries a risk of scarring. A primary goal of cosmetic lesion removal by a plastic surgeon is to minimise this. The final appearance depends on the removal method, the lesion's depth, and your skin’s natural healing process. Often, the result is a small, subtle mark that is less conspicuous than the original growth.

Can seborrheic keratosis turn into cancer?

Seborrheic keratoses are benign (non-cancerous) and do not become malignant. However, on rare occasions, a skin cancer can arise near or within an existing lesion, or mimic its appearance. For this reason, an accurate initial diagnosis by a qualified medical professional is essential before any removal is considered.

How much does seborrheic keratosis removal cost?

The cost for private seborrheic keratosis removal is based on several factors, including the number, size, and location of the lesions, as well as the specific technique required. A precise quotation will be provided during your personal consultation after Mr. Vijayan has assessed your individual case.

Can I have multiple lesions removed in one session?

Yes, it is often possible and efficient to remove several seborrheic keratoses during a single appointment. The suitability of treating multiple lesions at once will be determined during your consultation, based on an assessment of their location and the total scope of the procedure.

item.title: Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair: Simultaneous Treatment
item.dc:creator: Vijayan
item.content:encoded:
Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair: A Combined Solution

A tummy tuck and hernia repair is a combined surgical approach addressing both aesthetic and functional abdominal concerns. This guide explores the benefits of a single procedure, ideal candidate criteria, and the expected recovery timeline. It provides detailed insight into the specific types of hernias suitable for this treatment, the distinction between the tummy tuck and hernia correction, and the crucial role of the plastic surgeon in achieving a comprehensive and lasting result.

Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), is a Consultant Plastic Surgeon with extensive experience in abdominal wall surgery. He is a substantive NHS Consultant based in Stevenage, with a private practice across the region. To discuss your options with Mr. Roshan Vijayan, book a personal consultation at his practice serving patients across London, Hertfordshire, and Stevenage.

Table of Contents

  • Understanding the Dual-Benefit Tummy Tuck with Hernia Repair
  • What Are the Benefits of Combining These Procedures?
  • Who Is a Suitable Candidate for This Combined Surgery?
  • What Does the Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair Procedure Involve?
  • How Safe Is a Simultaneous Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair?
  • Navigating Your Recovery After Abdominal Surgery
  • What Realistic Outcomes Can You Expect from This Surgery?
  • Your Consultation for Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair in London

Understanding the Dual-Benefit Tummy Tuck with Hernia Repair

Yes, a hernia can be repaired during a tummy tuck. This combined surgical approach addresses both the functional issue of the hernia and the aesthetic concerns of excess abdominal skin and weakened muscles in a single procedure. A Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair provides a comprehensive treatment for individuals who have experienced significant changes to their abdomen, often due to pregnancy or weight loss.

The procedure essentially combines two distinct operations. The hernia repair component focuses on a specific medical issue: a weakness or hole in the abdominal wall that allows internal tissues to protrude, creating a noticeable bulge. This is a functional repair to restore the integrity of the muscle wall. The types of hernias most commonly addressed in this combined manner include umbilical (around the navel), epigastric (above the navel), and incisional (at the site of a previous surgical scar). The abdominoplasty, or tummy tuck, is the aesthetic component. It targets loose skin, removes stubborn fat deposits, and tightens the separated or weakened abdominal muscles (a condition known as diastasis recti). By performing them together, the surgeon can use a single incision to access and correct both issues, leading to a more streamlined recovery and a cohesive final result.

What Are the Benefits of Combining These Procedures?

Opting for a combined abdominal surgery offers several practical and clinical advantages over undergoing two separate operations. These dual procedure benefits are centred on efficiency, recovery, and overall outcome, making it a compelling option for suitable candidates.

A Single Surgical Event

The most significant benefit is undergoing surgery just once. This means one period of general anaesthesia, reducing the overall exposure and associated risks that come with multiple anaesthetics. It consolidates the logistical planning for the patient, involving a single hospital admission and one period of time off from work and daily activities.

One Cohesive Recovery Period

Recovery from any major surgery requires time and care. By combining the tummy tuck with the hernia repair, you also combine the recovery periods. Instead of enduring two separate downtimes—one for the hernia and another for the abdominoplasty—you will heal from both simultaneously. While the initial recovery may be intensive, it is ultimately more efficient than restarting the healing process months later for a second procedure.

Improved Aesthetic and Functional Outcome

A plastic surgeon can address both the underlying structural weakness of the hernia and the external appearance of the abdomen in one operation. This integrated approach allows for superior contouring. The muscle tightening (plication) performed during the tummy tuck can reinforce the hernia repair, potentially leading to a stronger and more durable result. The final scar is also singular; the incision required for a full tummy tuck provides excellent access for the hernia repair, avoiding the need for multiple scars on the abdomen.

Cost-Effectiveness

While the initial cost of a combined procedure is higher than for a single surgery, it is generally more economical than paying for two separate operations. Costs such as the surgeon’s fee, anaesthetist’s fee, and hospital facility charges are incurred only once, representing a considerable saving compared to staging the procedures separately.

Who Is a Suitable Candidate for This Combined Surgery?

Determining suitability for a combined tummy tuck and hernia repair involves a thorough assessment of your physical health, lifestyle, and surgical goals. An ideal candidate is someone who is troubled by both the functional symptoms of a hernia and the aesthetic appearance of a lax or protruding abdomen. However, several key criteria must be met to ensure the procedure is both safe and effective for you.

Key considerations for candidacy include:

  • Good General Health: You should be in good overall health with no underlying medical conditions that could impair healing or increase surgical risk. This will be evaluated through a pre-operative assessment.
  • Stable Weight: Candidates should be at or near their ideal body weight and have maintained it for at least six months. This procedure is for body contouring, not weight loss, and significant weight fluctuations post-surgery can compromise the results.
  • Non-Smoker: Smoking significantly impedes the healing process and increases the risk of complications such as poor wound healing and infection. You will be required to stop smoking for a significant period before and after surgery.
  • Realistic Expectations: It is vital to have a clear understanding of what the surgery can and cannot achieve. The goal is improvement, not an unachievable ideal. Mr. Roshan Vijayan will discuss the likely outcomes with you during your consultation.
  • Finished with Pregnancies: While not an absolute requirement, it is generally recommended that women considering this procedure have completed their families, as future pregnancies can stretch the abdominal muscles and skin, potentially reversing the surgical results.

The Role of a Specialist Plastic Surgeon

A combined tummy tuck and hernia repair is a complex procedure that requires expertise in both reconstructive and aesthetic surgery. A Consultant Plastic Surgeon is uniquely qualified to perform this surgery. Unlike a general surgeon who would focus solely on the hernia repair, a plastic surgeon has advanced training in managing soft tissues, contouring the abdomen, and optimising scar placement for the best possible aesthetic outcome. As an experienced plastic surgeon and an NHS Consultant, Mr. Roshan Vijayan, FRCS (Plast), possesses the skills to safely perform the hernia repair while delivering a refined, natural-looking abdominal contour.

What Does the Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair Procedure Involve?

The Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair is performed under general anaesthesia and typically takes between three to five hours, depending on the complexity of the case. The procedure is meticulously planned to address both the hernia correction and the abdominal contouring in a seamless sequence.

Surgical Steps

The operation generally follows a structured plan:

  1. The Incision: A horizontal incision is made across the lower abdomen, typically running from hip to hip, positioned low enough to be concealed by underwear or swimwear. This incision provides the necessary access to both the hernia and the abdominal muscles.
  2. Hernia Repair: The first functional step is the hernia correction. The protruding tissue is carefully returned to its proper position within the abdominal cavity. The weakness or defect in the abdominal wall is then repaired. Depending on the size and location of the hernia, this may involve stitching the muscle tissue together or reinforcing the area with a piece of surgical mesh for added strength and to reduce the likelihood of recurrence.
  3. Muscle Plication: The surgeon then addresses the separated abdominal muscles (diastasis recti). These muscles, which run vertically down the abdomen, are pulled back to the midline and sutured into a tighter, flatter position. This step is integral to the abdominoplasty (tummy tuck) component and helps to create a firmer abdominal wall and a narrower waistline.
  4. Skin and Fat Removal: Once the underlying structures are repaired, the excess skin and fat from the lower abdomen are pulled down. The surplus tissue is precisely measured and surgically excised. In some cases, liposuction may be used on the flanks or upper abdomen to further enhance the final contour.
  5. Navel Repositioning and Closure: A new opening is created for the navel, which is brought out and sutured into a natural-looking position. The initial incision is then carefully closed with sutures. Surgical drains may be placed temporarily to prevent fluid accumulation.

How Safe Is a Simultaneous Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair?

For a carefully selected patient in the hands of a qualified consultant plastic surgeon, combining a tummy tuck with a hernia repair is a well-established and generally safe procedure. The decision to combine surgeries is made after a comprehensive evaluation of your health status to ensure the benefits outweigh any potential risks. However, like any major surgery, it carries inherent risks that must be understood.

Mr. Vijayan prioritises patient safety and will discuss these potential complications with you in detail. Proactive measures are taken before, during, and after surgery to minimise these risks.

Potential Risks and Management

  • Infection: Any surgical incision carries a risk of infection. This occurs in a small percentage of cases and is typically managed effectively with antibiotics. Strict sterile techniques are used during surgery to minimise this risk.
  • Bleeding or Haematoma: Some bleeding is expected, but a haematoma (a collection of blood under the skin) may occasionally form, sometimes requiring a return to the operating theatre for drainage.
  • Seroma: This is a collection of fluid that can accumulate under the skin. It is one of the more common issues after a tummy tuck but can usually be managed simply with drainage in the clinic during follow-up appointments.
  • Blood Clots (DVT/PE): Deep Vein Thrombosis (a clot in the leg) and Pulmonary Embolism (a clot in the lung) are rare but serious risks associated with any major surgery. Preventative measures, such as compression stockings, calf pumps during surgery, and early mobilisation, are standard protocol to reduce this risk.
  • Poor Scarring: While every effort is made to place the scar discreetly and ensure it heals well, individual healing varies. Some patients may develop thickened (hypertrophic) or keloid scars, which may require further treatment.
  • Hernia Recurrence: There is a small risk that the hernia may return in the future. Using surgical mesh for the repair can reduce this risk, as can following post-operative activity restrictions.

Navigating Your Recovery After Abdominal Surgery

Recovery is a gradual process that requires patience and adherence to post-operative instructions. A successful outcome is highly dependent on how you manage this period. You should expect to feel tired and sore for the first week or two, with discomfort managed by prescribed pain relief medication.

The First Two Weeks

You will likely stay in the hospital for one to two nights for monitoring. Upon discharge, you will need someone to drive you home and assist you for the first few days. You will be advised to walk in a slightly bent-over position to avoid straining the incision line. Light, short walks around the house are encouraged from day one to promote circulation and reduce the risk of blood clots. You will wear a compression garment or abdominal binder continuously. This garment supports the repaired tissues, minimises swelling, and helps the skin conform to your new abdominal shape. Strenuous activity, heavy lifting (including children), and driving are prohibited during this initial phase.

Weeks Three to Six

By this stage, you should feel more comfortable and be able to stand up straighter. Swelling and bruising will continue to subside, although some residual swelling can persist for several months. Depending on the nature of your job, you may be able to return to desk-based work after two to three weeks. You can gradually increase your activity levels, but you must continue to avoid vigorous exercise and heavy lifting until you are cleared by your surgeon, typically around the six-week mark.

Beyond Six Weeks

At your six-week follow-up appointment, if your healing is progressing well, you will likely be permitted to resume most of your normal activities, including more strenuous exercise. It is important to reintroduce exercise gradually to rebuild your core strength. The incision scar will continue to mature and fade over the next 12 to 18 months, changing from red or pink to a paler, less noticeable line.

What Realistic Outcomes Can You Expect from This Surgery?

A combined tummy tuck and hernia repair can produce substantial and lasting improvements to the function and appearance of your abdomen. The primary outcome is a flatter, firmer, and more toned abdominal profile. The procedure directly addresses the physical bulge of the hernia while also removing loose, excess skin and tightening the underlying muscles that may have been stretched by pregnancy or weight changes.

What the Surgery Can Achieve

  • Functional Repair: The hernia will be corrected, alleviating associated symptoms such as pain or discomfort and restoring the integrity of the abdominal wall.
  • Aesthetic Enhancement: The surgery creates a smoother, more contoured abdomen by removing redundant skin and tightening the muscular corset.
  • Improved Core Stability: Repairing diastasis recti can lead to improved posture and may help to alleviate some types of lower back pain associated with a weak core.
  • Increased Confidence: Many patients report a significant boost in self-esteem and feel more comfortable in clothing and swimwear.

Limitations and Long-Term Maintenance

It is important to have realistic expectations. This surgery will result in a permanent scar across the lower abdomen, though it is placed to be hidden by most underwear. While the fat cells and skin removed are gone permanently, the results are not entirely immune to future life events. Significant weight gain can stretch the remaining skin and compromise the aesthetic outcome. Similarly, a future pregnancy will re-stretch the repaired muscles and skin. To maintain your results for the long term, a commitment to a stable weight through a balanced diet and regular exercise is essential. This will help preserve the contoured shape achieved through surgery and support the durability of the hernia repair.

Your Consultation for Tummy Tuck and Hernia Repair in London

The first step towards understanding if this combined procedure is right for you is a private consultation. This meeting provides an opportunity for you to discuss your concerns and goals in a supportive and confidential environment. Mr. Roshan Vijayan will conduct a thorough physical examination, review your medical history, and explain the surgical options available to you, including the potential benefits and risks involved.

He will listen to your expectations and provide an honest assessment of the results you can realistically anticipate. This is your time to ask questions and gather all the information you need to make a well-informed decision about your care. You will leave the consultation with a clear understanding of the procedure, the recovery process, and the associated costs.

To discuss your options with Mr. Roshan Vijayan, book a personal consultation at his practice serving patients across London, Hertfordshire, and Stevenage.

Frequently Asked Questions About Combined Procedures

Will the NHS or private insurance cover a combined tummy tuck and hernia repair?

In the UK, hernia repair may be covered by the NHS or private insurance as a medical necessity. The abdominoplasty (tummy tuck) component, however, is almost always considered cosmetic and is therefore self-funded. The costs are handled separately for each part.

You should clarify coverage with your insurance provider. Our practice can provide the necessary clinical information regarding the hernia repair for your insurance claim.

What types of hernias are suitable for repair during a tummy tuck?

The most common hernias addressed during this combined procedure are umbilical (at the navel) and ventral or incisional hernias, which appear on the abdominal wall, often at the site of a previous surgical scar. Their location makes them accessible during an abdominoplasty.

Who performs the different parts of this combined surgery?

As a Consultant Plastic Surgeon with comprehensive training in abdominal wall reconstruction, Mr. Roshan Vijayan is qualified to perform both the hernia repair and the abdominoplasty. This integrated approach ensures a cohesive surgical plan managed by a single specialist surgeon.

Are the risks higher when combining these two operations?

Combining the procedures into a single operation means you undergo general anaesthesia and a recovery period only once. The overall risk profile is not considered significantly higher than having two separate surgeries. All surgical risks will be discussed in detail during your consultation.

When can I return to exercise after a tummy tuck with hernia repair?

Gentle walking is encouraged shortly after surgery, but strenuous activities and core exercises must be avoided for at least six to eight weeks. This period is crucial to allow the repaired abdominal muscles and hernia site to heal properly before being placed under strain.

How long do the results of a combined procedure last?

The results can be very long-lasting. A hernia repair is intended to be a permanent solution, while the removal of excess skin is also permanent. However, significant future weight changes or pregnancies can stretch the skin and abdominal muscles, altering the aesthetic outcome.

Maintaining a stable weight is the most effective way to preserve your surgical results.
